metadata.title: R-5 High-Rise Residential Tower - Katipunan Avenue, Quezon City

scenario_brief.location: Along Katipunan Avenue (RROW 20m), near Ateneo/UP, Quezon City
scenario_brief.building_official_requirement: Minimum 6.0m setback on all sides for buildings exceeding 15m in height

step_2_setback_buildable.note: Building Official prescribed setback (75m height building) governs over PSO AMBF

step_3_governing_ambf.note: Setback-limited area is smaller; applies to podium max footprint

step_4_tgfa_computation.note: TGFA includes all floor areas (podium parking + tower residential)

step_5_gfa_computation.note: GFA excludes parking areas per standard definition

step_6_flar_verification.note: FLAR within allowed range for R-5

step_7_bhl_verification.note: R-5 BHL minimum is 48m (not a height limit but zoning minimum); building at 75m satisfies both

step_8_open_space.note: ISA + USA = minimum open space allocation

questions.question_stem: What is the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) derived from the Percentage Site Occupancy (PSO) for this R-5 lot?

rationale.correct: AMBF from PSO = TLA × PSO = 2,500 × 0.70 = 1,750 sqm. This is the maximum footprint allowed by zoning regulations before applying setback restrictions.
rationale.distractor_0: This is 50% of TLA, confusing PSO with a different percentage or misapplying the formula.
rationale.distractor_1: This is the buildable area after applying setbacks (6.0m all sides), which is a separate limit that governs in this case because 1,444 < 1,750. Students may confuse this with AMBF from PSO.
rationale.distractor_2: This is the entire TLA; AMBF cannot exceed TLA but is further limited by PSO percentage.
rationale.takeaway: AMBF from PSO is calculated before considering setbacks. The governing AMBF is the minimum of PSO-derived and setback-limited areas.

questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control

questions.question_stem: The Building Official prescribes a 6.0m setback on all sides (front, rear, both sides) for buildings exceeding 15m in height. What is the maximum buildable footprint after applying these setbacks?

rationale.correct: Setback reductions: Width = 50m - 6.0m (front) - 6.0m (rear) = 38m. Depth = 50m - 6.0m (east) - 6.0m (west) = 38m. Buildable area = 38 × 38 = 1,444 sqm. This is a TRAP: the Building Official's prescribed setback (6.0m all sides) overrides the standard setback table (which would use 3.0m for sides in the 12-15m bracket). Students using standard table (3.0m) would get 1,764 sqm (44 × 44).
rationale.distractor_0: This results from using standard table setbacks (3.0m sides, 6.0m front/rear), yielding 44m × 44m = 1,936 sqm. However, the Building Official's prescribed setback takes precedence.
rationale.distractor_1: This is approximately the result of using different setback combinations or mathematical errors in dimension reduction.
rationale.distractor_2: This assumes uniform 4.0m setback or other incorrect values.
rationale.takeaway: When a Building Official prescribes setbacks for high-rise buildings, those prescribed values OVERRIDE standard regulatory tables. Always check for special requirements in the scenario brief.

solution_steps: Note the Building Official's prescribed setback: 6.0m all sides
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Setbacks and Firewalls; Building Official's approval memo

questions.question_stem: Which AMBF value governs the design of this building—the one derived from PSO or the one constrained by setbacks—and why?
options: PSO AMBF (1,750 sqm) governs because zoning regulations take precedence over architectural setbacks.
Setback AMBF (1,444 sqm) governs because it is the smaller, more restrictive limit.
Both apply independently; use 1,750 sqm for footprint and 1,444 sqm for tower.
Setback AMBF (1,444 sqm) governs only if the Building Official mandate is documented in writing.

rationale.correct: The governing AMBF is the minimum of PSO-derived (1,750 sqm) and setback-constrained (1,444 sqm) areas. Since 1,444 < 1,750, the setback limit is more restrictive and governs. The podium footprint of 1,200 sqm fits within this limit. The TRAP is understanding that BOTH limits apply and the smaller one is binding.
rationale.distractor_0: Zoning PSO sets a maximum but can be further restricted by geometric constraints like setbacks. PSO does not automatically take precedence.
rationale.distractor_1: These are not independent limits. You cannot use 1,750 sqm for part of the building and 1,444 sqm for another; the maximum possible footprint at any level is 1,444 sqm.
rationale.distractor_2: The Building Official's requirement, once documented (as in this scenario), is enforceable and takes immediate effect; it does not require additional documentation.
rationale.takeaway: Development control parameters (PSO, setbacks) create overlapping limits. Design must satisfy ALL constraints simultaneously. The most restrictive constraint governs.

solution_steps: Identify both AMBF limits: PSO = 1,750 sqm, Setback = 1,444 sqm
Verify proposed podium footprint (1,200 sqm) ≤ 1,444 sqm ✓
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control Parameters

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) for this 25-storey building with a 3-storey parking podium (1,200 sqm footprint) and 22-storey residential tower (750 sqm footprint).

rationale.correct: TGFA = (Podium floors × Podium footprint) + (Tower floors × Tower footprint) = (3 × 1,200) + (22 × 750) = 3,600 + 16,500 = 20,100 sqm. TGFA includes all floors regardless of use (parking + residential). This is a TRAP: students often use tower footprint for all 25 floors (750 × 25 = 18,750 sqm), ignoring the podium's larger footprint.
rationale.distractor_0: This is the TRAP value: 750 sqm × 25 floors = 18,750 sqm. This assumes the tower footprint applies throughout the building, ignoring the larger podium footprint (1,200 sqm). COMMON MISTAKE.
rationale.distractor_1: This is the GFA, excluding parking: 20,100 - 3,600 = 16,500 sqm. Students confuse TGFA with GFA.
rationale.distractor_2: This results from other incorrect floor count or footprint combinations; also exceeds the FLAR range.
rationale.takeaway: TGFA computation for podium-tower buildings requires separate calculation of podium and tower contributions. Parking areas are INCLUDED in TGFA but EXCLUDED from GFA.

solution_steps: Note: Parking (3,600 sqm) is included in TGFA but excluded from GFA
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule I, Definitions; Development Control

questions.question_stem: What is the Gross Floor Area (GFA) of this building, and why does it differ from TGFA?
options: 16,500 sqm (excludes parking, which is not 'occupied' space)
20,100 sqm (same as TGFA; all floors count toward occupancy)
3,600 sqm (only parking areas count as enclosed space)

rationale.correct: GFA = TGFA - Parking areas = 20,100 - 3,600 = 16,500 sqm. Parking areas (covered or uncovered) are excluded from GFA under standard definitions because parking is considered ancillary/support space, not primary occupancy space. GFA is used for occupancy classification and egress calculations.
rationale.distractor_0: See correct answer.
rationale.distractor_1: TGFA and GFA are NOT the same. TGFA includes all enclosed areas; GFA excludes parking. The distinction is critical for occupancy classification.
rationale.distractor_2: Parking is the majority of the podium, but only podium parking is excluded—tower residential areas are counted in GFA.
rationale.distractor_3: Mechanical/MEP spaces may have exceptions, but the primary exclusion here is parking, which accounts for 3,600 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: GFA ≠ TGFA. Parking exclusion is standard. Understand the distinction for occupancy classification (uses GFA) vs. development control (uses TGFA).

solution_steps: Identify parking areas: podium 3 floors × 1,200 sqm = 3,600 sqm
Verify: GFA is used for occupancy classification, parking excluded
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule I, Definitions; GFA definition

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Floor-to-Area Ratio (FLAR) for this building and verify compliance with the R-5 zoning requirement.

rationale.correct: FLAR = TGFA ÷ TLA = 20,100 ÷ 2,500 = 8.04. The R-5 zoning range is 3.6–9.0, so 8.04 is compliant. TRAP: students may calculate 750 sqm × 25 ÷ 2,500 = 7.5 (using wrong TGFA), or use GFA ÷ TLA = 16,500 ÷ 2,500 = 6.6 (correct ratio but using GFA instead of TGFA for zoning compliance).
rationale.distractor_0: This may result from an intermediate calculation error or rounding.
rationale.distractor_1: Using GFA instead of TGFA: 16,500 ÷ 2,500 = 6.6. While GFA-based FLAR is lower and could appear conservative, development control uses TGFA for FLAR verification.
rationale.distractor_2: This is the TRAP from using wrong TGFA (750 × 25 = 18,750): 18,750 ÷ 2,500 = 7.5. Still within range but based on incorrect floor area.
rationale.distractor_3: This result (9.24) would come from computing TGFA as (2 × 1,200) + (23 × 750) = 19,650 ÷ 2,500, or similar error, and exceeds the maximum allowed.
rationale.takeaway: FLAR for zoning compliance uses TGFA (not GFA) divided by TLA. Both parking and residential floors count. Verify result against zoning FLAR range.

solution_steps: Identify TGFA = 20,100 sqm (correct calculation from previous questions)
Check R-5 range: 3.6–9.0. Result 8.04 is within range ✓
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control Parameters; FLAR definition

questions.question_stem: What is the required Intensive Space Area (ISA) for this 2,500 sqm R-5 lot?

rationale.correct: ISA = TLA × ISA% = 2,500 × 0.10 = 250 sqm. The scenario specifies ISA% = 10% for R-5. ISA is used for active recreation, play areas, or landscaped activity zones (not passive/green space).
rationale.distractor_0: This is 6% of TLA; the scenario specifies 10%.
rationale.distractor_1: This is 7% of TLA; incorrect percentage.
rationale.distractor_2: This is USA%, not ISA. USA = 20%, so 2,500 × 0.20 = 500 sqm. Students confuse ISA with USA.
rationale.takeaway: ISA (Intensive Space Area) is distinct from USA (Unstructured Space Area). ISA is active recreation; USA is passive/green. Both are required minimums and sum to Total OS (Open Space).

questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control; Open Space Standards

questions.question_stem: What is the total required Open Space (OS) for this lot, combining both ISA and USA?

rationale.correct: Total OS = ISA + USA = 250 + 500 = 750 sqm. Both ISA and USA are mandatory minimums and must be provided separately within the lot (or as approved by the Building Official, in adjacent public space).
rationale.distractor_0: This is ISA alone; does not account for USA requirement.
rationale.distractor_1: This is USA alone; does not account for ISA requirement.
rationale.distractor_2: This is the average; students may incorrectly think one or the other is required, not both.
rationale.takeaway: Open Space is a dual requirement: ISA (active) + USA (passive). Both must be satisfied. Total OS = ISA + USA, a cumulative obligation.

solution_steps: Identify USA = 500 sqm (from scenario, 20% of TLA)
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Open Space Standards

questions.question_stem: Verify that the building height of 75m (25 floors × 3.0m floor-to-floor) complies with the R-5 Building Height Limit (BHL). What is the BHL range for R-5 zoning?
options: No height limit for R-5 zoning

rationale.correct: The R-5 BHL range is 48m–180m, permitting high-rise residential development. A 75m building (25 × 3.0m) falls within this range and is compliant. The range indicates a MINIMUM of 48m (buildings under 48m may be classified as lower zoning) and a MAXIMUM of 180m. TRAP: students may confuse 48m as a height target rather than a minimum threshold, or use R-3 BHL (15m) or other classifications incorrectly.
rationale.distractor_0: This is typical for R-2 or low-density zoning. R-5 permits much greater heights.
rationale.distractor_1: This might apply to mid-rise zones; R-5 exceeds this range significantly.
rationale.distractor_2: While R-5 does not have a strict unlimited height limit in all jurisdictions, it does have a prescribed range. The 48m–180m range is typical for high-rise residential.
rationale.takeaway: Each zoning classification has a prescribed BHL range. For R-5 high-rise residential, the range is 48m–180m. Verify building height against this range.

questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control Parameters; R-5 Zoning Standards

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Maximum Area Coverage (MACA) percentage for this R-5 lot and verify if the podium footprint (1,200 sqm) complies.
options: 75% (MACA = average of PSO and open space)

rationale.correct: MACA = PSO + ISA = 70% + 10% = 80%. This means up to 80% of the lot may be covered by structures (building + ISA improvements) if ISA is counted as structured/hardscape. The podium at 1,200 sqm covers 1,200÷2,500 = 48%, well below 80%. Compliance verified. TRAP: students may confuse MACA with PSO alone (70%) or with total open space allocation (90%).
rationale.distractor_0: PSO (70%) is the primary site occupancy limit, but MACA adds ISA allowance for a total of 80%.
rationale.distractor_1: If students include USA (20%) instead of ISA, they get 90%. However, USA is unstructured/green space and not part of MACA; ISA (hardscape, active recreation) can count toward MACA.
rationale.distractor_2: This would result from averaging PSO and total open space percentage incorrectly.
rationale.takeaway: MACA (Maximum Area Coverage) = PSO + ISA. This allows up to 80% of the lot to be covered (building + ISA improvements), with the remaining space split between USA and street setbacks.

solution_steps: Verify podium footprint compliance: 1,200 sqm ÷ 2,500 sqm = 48% < 80% ✓
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Development Control; Area Coverage Standards

questions.question_stem: The scenario states that the Building Official requires a 6.0m setback on all sides for buildings exceeding 15m in height. This requirement applies to this 75m building. How does this setback requirement differ from the standard setback table for buildings in the 12m–15m height bracket?
options: The Building Official setback (6.0m all sides) is more restrictive; the standard table allows 3.0m for side yards in the 12–15m bracket.
The Building Official setback and standard table are identical; no difference.
The standard table is more restrictive, requiring 8.0m front setbacks; the Building Official allows 6.0m.
Setbacks do not apply to buildings exceeding 15m; only PSO limits apply.

rationale.correct: The standard setback table (for buildings 12–15m) prescribes: front = 6.0m, sides = 3.0m each, rear = 3.0m. The Building Official's requirement (for this 75m building) is: all sides = 6.0m. This is MORE RESTRICTIVE on the sides (6.0m vs. 3.0m). When an official mandates tighter setbacks, that mandate overrides the standard table. TRAP: students may assume the standard table applies, calculating 44m × 44m = 1,936 sqm instead of the correct 38m × 38m = 1,444 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: See correct answer.
rationale.distractor_1: They are different. The Building Official's prescription (documented in scenario brief) takes precedence over general regulatory tables.
rationale.distractor_2: The standard table does not prescribe 8.0m for any 12–15m bracket; this is incorrect.
rationale.distractor_3: Setbacks always apply to surface-level area calculations; BHL does not eliminate setback requirements.
rationale.takeaway: Official prescriptions override standard tables. Always check the scenario brief for special Building Official requirements. Site-specific mandates are binding.

solution_steps: Identify standard table setback for 12–15m bracket: front 6.0m, sides 3.0m, rear 3.0m
Identify Building Official prescribed setback: 6.0m all sides
Compare: Building Official's side setback (6.0m) > standard (3.0m), making the official requirement MORE restrictive
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Setbacks and Firewalls; Building Official Authority

questions.question_stem: The lot is rectangular, 50m wide (along Katipunan Avenue to the south) and 50m deep (toward the north, where the university is located). How many setbacks apply, and which boundary faces the primary road?
options: Two setbacks (front and rear); the front (south) faces Katipunan Avenue.
Four setbacks (front, rear, both sides); the front (south) faces Katipunan Avenue.
Three setbacks (front and both sides only); rear setback waived for university adjacency.
One setback (front only); interior lot boundaries do not require setbacks.

rationale.correct: Four setbacks apply: front (south, along Katipunan Avenue), rear (north, toward university), and both sides (east and west, toward adjacent R-5 residential). The front setback (south) is along the primary road (Katipunan Avenue, 20m RROW). All four boundaries require setbacks per standard regulations unless specifically exempted (which the scenario does not indicate).
rationale.distractor_0: Two setbacks (front and rear) neglect the side yard setbacks on east and west boundaries.
rationale.distractor_1: The scenario does not waive rear setback for university adjacency; institutional adjacency does not override setback requirements.
rationale.distractor_2: Interior lots (not facing a road) may have fewer setback requirements in some jurisdictions, but this lot is bounded by Katipunan Avenue and is not an interior lot.
rationale.takeaway: A rectangular corner/boulevard lot typically has four setback requirements (all boundaries). Understand lot orientation and identify which boundary is 'front' (primary road). All boundaries require setbacks unless explicitly exempted.

solution_steps: Identify lot boundaries: south (frontage, 50m), north (50m), east (50m), west (50m)
Identify road boundary: Katipunan Avenue along south (RROW 20m)
Designate: Front = south (road), Rear = north, Sides = east and west
Conclusion: Four setbacks apply (front, rear, east, west)
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Setbacks and Firewalls; Lot Orientation

questions.question_stem: Given the 6.0m setback on all sides, calculate the exact buildable dimensions (width and depth) and the resulting buildable footprint.

rationale.correct: Buildable width = 50m - 6.0m (front) - 6.0m (rear) = 38m. Buildable depth = 50m - 6.0m (east) - 6.0m (west) = 38m. Footprint = 38m × 38m = 1,444 sqm. This is the correct calculation applying the Building Official's 6.0m setback on all sides.
rationale.distractor_0: See correct answer.
rationale.distractor_1: Width: 40m results from 50 - 5 - 5 = 40, using incorrect 5.0m setbacks. Footprint: 40 × 40 = 1,600 sqm.
rationale.distractor_2: Width: 42m results from 50 - 4 - 4 = 42, using incorrect 4.0m setbacks. Footprint: 42 × 42 = 1,764 sqm. This is the setback calculation using standard table (3.0m sides, not 6.0m).
rationale.distractor_3: Width: 44m results from 50 - 3 - 3 = 44, using only 3.0m setbacks. Footprint: 44 × 44 = 1,936 sqm. This is also a standard table result (incorrect for this scenario).
rationale.takeaway: Setback reduction is applied twice (once on each side of each dimension). Careful arithmetic: 50 - 6 - 6 = 38, not 44 or 42. Verify against the prescribed setbacks.

questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule VIII, Setbacks and Firewalls

questions.question_stem: This building uses a podium-tower configuration with a 3-storey parking podium (1,200 sqm footprint) and a 22-storey residential tower (750 sqm footprint). What is the primary zoning advantage of this configuration?
options: Maximizes residential units by limiting parking to the podium.
Reduces FLAR by concentrating residential floor area above the podium, allowing the tower to have a smaller footprint while maintaining density.
Eliminates the need for setbacks by recessing the tower above the podium.

rationale.correct: The podium-tower configuration allows the larger podium (1,200 sqm) to provide parking while the tower (750 sqm) concentrates residential units vertically. This reduces the building's footprint constraint (750 sqm tower << 1,444 sqm buildable limit) while keeping FLAR within the 3.6–9.0 range. The tower's setback from podium edges is common architectural practice (visual/structural) but setback legal minimums still apply to the podium edges. TRAP: students may think the tower's recess eliminates setback requirements, which it does not.
rationale.distractor_0: While parking concentration is a feature, the zoning advantage is not simply maximizing units but achieving compliance with multiple constraints simultaneously.
rationale.distractor_1: Tower recession can improve aesthetics and reduce wind effects, but it does not eliminate setbacks; the podium still requires setbacks from lot lines.
rationale.distractor_2: Street-level retail is not mentioned in this scenario; the podium is parking-focused.
rationale.takeaway: Podium-tower configurations balance large podium footprints (for parking/support) with smaller tower footprints (for residential density), allowing high-rise development while managing FLAR and site coverage constraints.

solution_steps: Identify podium footprint (1,200 sqm) vs. tower footprint (750 sqm)
Recognize that larger podium accommodates parking while smaller tower concentrates residential units
Conclusion: Podium-tower separates functions vertically, balancing constraints
questions.code_citation: ale-dsgn-003-02-multi-family-high-rise-residential

questions.question_stem: The tower has 22 residential floors (750 sqm each) providing space for a mix of unit types: studios (28 sqm), 1BR (45 sqm), 2BR (70 sqm), and 3BR (100 sqm). Assuming an average unit size of 60 sqm and 15% common area, how many units approximately fit per typical floor?

rationale.correct: Per floor NRA (net rentable area) = 750 sqm × (1 - 0.15 common area) = 637.5 sqm. Average unit size = 60 sqm. Units per floor ≈ 637.5 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.6. With corridor and common area inefficiency, realistic count is 10–12 units per floor, or with tighter spacing, 12–14. Using the conservative middle estimate of 12–14 units per floor is typical. TRAP: students may forget to deduct common area or use gross area (750 sqm), yielding 12.5 units (incorrect because it ignores the 15% common area allocation).
rationale.distractor_0: This underestimates; it assumes very large average units or higher common area deduction.
rationale.distractor_1: This is reasonable but on the lower end; 15% common area deduction and 60 sqm average should yield slightly higher counts.
rationale.distractor_2: This accounts for 15% common area and 60 sqm average unit: 750 × 0.85 = 637.5 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.6 ≈ 10–12 after rounding, but the range 12–14 represents a typical achievable count with unit mix flexibility.
rationale.distractor_3: This overestimates; it neglects common area or assumes average unit < 50 sqm.
rationale.takeaway: For residential floors, deduct common areas (corridors, lobbies, MEP) before dividing by unit size. Typical unit counts per floor are 10–15 units for mid-rise residential, depending on mix.

solution_steps: Identify tower floor area: 750 sqm gross
Divide by average unit size (60 sqm): 637.5 ÷ 60 = 10.625 units
With practical spacing, achieve 12–14 units per floor
questions.code_citation: ale-dsgn-003-02-multi-family-high-rise-residential

questions.question_stem: What percentage of the 22 tower residential floors should be allocated to common/amenity spaces such as a swimming pool and gym? Typical high-rise residential developments allocate 1–2 floors for such amenities.
options: Amenity floors are not deducted; they are in addition to the 22 residential floors

rationale.correct: 1 floor out of 22 = 1÷22 ≈ 4.5%. Two floors = 2÷22 ≈ 9%. The scenario mentions 'amenities: swimming pool, gym, function room (at podium roof deck level).' If these are provided at the podium level (top of parking garage, typical for towers), they may not consume a full tower floor. If one residential floor is converted to amenities, allocate 4–9%. If two floors, allocate 9–14%. The scenario suggests podium roof deck, so minimal tower floor impact. Answer is approximately 4–9% for 1 floor.
rationale.distractor_0: See correct answer.
rationale.distractor_1: This assumes 2 dedicated amenity floors, increasing the percentage to 9–14%. Possible but depends on project scope.
rationale.distractor_2: Three floors would be 13.6%, less common for a 22-floor tower unless very amenity-rich.
rationale.distractor_3: In some developments, amenity floors are indeed separate from the unit count. However, the scenario specifies '22-storey residential tower,' implying 22 floors are available for allocation (whether units or amenities). The question presumes they are carved out of the 22.
rationale.takeaway: Amenity floors are typically 5–10% of total residential floors for mid-rise buildings. Allocate realistically; high-rise developments rarely exceed 10% amenity allocation.

solution_steps: Assume 1 amenity floor (swimming pool, gym, function room typical allocation)
questions.code_citation: ale-dsgn-003-02-multi-family-high-rise-residential

questions.question_stem: What is the occupancy classification of this 25-storey residential condominium tower according to the National Building Code (based on GFA of 16,500 sqm)?
options: Occupancy Group R-1 (hotels and similar transient residential)
Occupancy Group R-2 (residential with independent units, not more than 16 storeys)
Occupancy Group R-3 (residential with independent units, more than 16 storeys)

rationale.correct: R-3 is the occupancy classification for residential buildings with independent living units exceeding 16 storeys in height. This building has 25 storeys, placing it in R-3. The GFA (16,500 sqm, excluding parking) is the relevant area for occupancy classification. TRAP: students may confuse R-2 (up to 16 storeys, also called multi-family) with R-3 (above 16 storeys). The building height (25 storeys > 16 storeys) determines R-3 classification.
rationale.distractor_0: R-1 is for hotels and transient residential use (guests stay temporarily), not permanent residential condominiums.
rationale.distractor_1: R-2 applies to residential buildings up to 16 storeys. This building exceeds 16 storeys (has 25 storeys), so it is classified as R-3.
rationale.distractor_2: This is a zoning classification (R-5 residential zone), not an occupancy classification. Occupancy and zoning are distinct.
rationale.takeaway: Occupancy classification (R-1, R-2, R-3) is based on building height and use type. R-3 applies to residential buildings with 17+ storeys. Building code egress, fire protection, and structural requirements vary by occupancy.

solution_steps: Identify use type: residential with independent living units (condo)
Check occupancy brackets: R-2 up to 16 storeys, R-3 for 17+ storeys
questions.code_citation: National Building Code, Rule I, Occupancy Classifications

questions.question_stem: Per PD 1096 (Accessibility Code), how many elevators are required for a 25-storey residential tower?
options: One elevator (minimum for any building with storeys)
Two elevators (minimum for buildings with 5–10 storeys)
Three elevators (minimum for buildings with more than 10 storeys)
Four elevators (for buildings 20+ storeys, plus at least one for freight)

rationale.correct: PD 1096 requires a minimum of two elevators for buildings with 5 or more storeys, and three elevators for buildings with more than 10 storeys (or two elevators + two hoists). At 25 storeys, this building requires a minimum of three elevators. Additionally, a freight/service elevator may be required, depending on building code and size. The base requirement is 3 passenger elevators minimum.
rationale.distractor_0: One elevator is insufficient; PD 1096 mandates multiple elevators for buildings above 5 storeys.
rationale.distractor_1: Two elevators is the minimum for buildings with 5–10 storeys. At 25 storeys (>10), three elevators are required.
rationale.distractor_2: Four elevators might be appropriate for a 25-storey tower for functional capacity and redundancy, but it is not the minimum code requirement.
rationale.takeaway: Elevator requirements scale with building height. PD 1096 specifies: 2 min for 5+ storeys, 3 min for 11+ storeys. High-rise buildings often provide more elevators for passenger volume and zone service.

solution_steps: Check PD 1096 requirements: 5+ storeys = 2 elevators, 10+ storeys = 3 elevators
Apply to 25 storeys: 25 > 10 → minimum 3 elevators required
Verify: May also provide freight/service elevator for residential use
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Accessibility Code of the Philippines

questions.question_stem: For a 25-storey residential condominium in Quezon City, what is the typical parking requirement per unit, and how many parking spaces does the proposed 250-space facility provide if the building accommodates approximately 280 units (22 floors × 12.7 units/floor)?
options: 1.0 space per unit required; 250 spaces provides 0.89 spaces/unit (under-parked)
1.5 spaces per unit required; 250 spaces provides 0.89 spaces/unit (significantly under-parked)
2.0 spaces per unit required; 250 spaces provides 0.89 spaces/unit (severely under-parked)
0.5 spaces per unit required; 250 spaces provides 0.89 spaces/unit (over-parked)

rationale.correct: MMDA Parking Guidelines (typical for Metro Manila including QC) require approximately 1.0–1.2 parking spaces per residential unit for mid-to-high-end condominiums. If 280 units ÷ 250 spaces = 0.89 spaces/unit, the facility is UNDER the standard requirement by about 11%. However, some jurisdictions accept 0.75–1.0 spaces/unit for high-rise residential in dense urban areas (Quezon City may have flexibility). At face value, 1.0 space/unit required vs. 0.89 provided shows under-parking. TRAP: students may assume 2.0 spaces/unit (suburban standard) or 1.5 spaces/unit (mixed-use), making the parking ratio appear more deficient than it actually is.
rationale.distractor_0: See correct answer.
rationale.distractor_1: 1.5 spaces per unit is typical for suburban residential; 250 spaces for 280 units (0.89/unit) would be significantly under-parked.
rationale.distractor_2: 2.0 spaces per unit is typical for suburban low-density residential or commercial; for high-rise urban residential, this is excessive.
rationale.distractor_3: 0.5 spaces per unit would be unrealistically low for residential; even transit-rich urban areas require 0.75+ spaces/unit.
